title: Found Again: My Beloved Is Mine
summary: The daughters of Jerusalem offer to help the woman search for her beloved, and she answers that he has gone down to his garden and that they belong to each other. He praises her again, calling her more striking than a city and more unique than all the queens of a royal court. The chapter ends with a puzzling scene in a nut orchard and a call for the Shulammite to come back so that others may look at her.
story: Chapter 5 ended with a painful scene: the woman hesitated to open the door at night, her beloved withdrew, and she searched the city for him, was beaten by the watchmen, and begged the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she was faint with love. When they asked what made her beloved better than others, she answered with a head-to-toe description of him (5:10-16). Chapter 6 picks up at once. The friends now ask where he has gone, and her answer shows that the separation was never as final as it felt: he is in his garden, and she belongs to him. The poem then returns to his voice, with praise that repeats lines from chapter 4 almost word for word, as though the relationship has been restored and the earlier words of admiration can be said again. The book is moving toward its last great statements about love in chapter 8, and this chapter shows love surviving a rupture.
historical:
The Song of Songs gives no clear historical events, and its date and authorship are debated. The heading in 1:1 connects it with Solomon, who reigned in the tenth century BC, but the Hebrew phrase can mean by Solomon, for Solomon, or about Solomon. Some scholars accept Solomonic authorship or at least an early core; others point to features of the language (such as a shortened form of the relative pronoun and some words that look like Persian or Greek loanwords) and date the book to the Persian or Hellenistic period, after the exile. Many see it as a collection of love poems, perhaps gathered over time.

This chapter does carry a few historical echoes. Tirzah (verse 4) was an early royal city of the northern kingdom of Israel before King Omri moved the capital to Samaria in the ninth century BC (1 Kings 16:23-24), and its name means something like pleasing. Pairing it with Jerusalem sets the two great capitals side by side, which some take as a sign of an early date and others as simple poetic choice. The sixty queens and eighty concubines (verse 8) evoke a royal harem like Solomon's, which 1 Kings 11:3 puts at seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. Gilead, east of the Jordan, was known for its pasture and flocks.
cultural:
The imagery is pastoral and horticultural. A man pasturing his flock among the lilies, beds of spices, and gardens were ordinary sights in the hill country, and in love poetry across the ancient Near East the garden was a common image of the beloved woman and of intimacy. Egyptian love songs from the second millennium BC use similar pictures of gardens, trees, and fragrance, and they also call lovers brother and sister, as the Song does elsewhere. The comparisons in verses 5 to 7 sound odd to modern ears but were meant as compliments: hair flowing like goats streaming down a hillside, teeth white and complete like washed ewes each with its twin (in a world without dentistry, a full set of teeth was a mark of beauty), and a face glowing like the inside of a pomegranate.

Verse 4's comparison to troops with banners, and verse 10's to dawn, moon, sun, and stars, show that her beauty is not merely pretty. It is overwhelming, even a little frightening, the way an army or the night sky can be. The word translated majestic can carry a sense of awe. Verse 13's Shulammite is the first time the woman has a title. Its meaning is debated: a woman from the village of Shunem (compare Abishag the Shunammite in 1 Kings 1:3), a feminine form matching the name Solomon, or a name connected with shalom, peace. The dance of Mahanaim is also obscure; Mahanaim, a town in Gilead, means two camps (Genesis 32:2), and the phrase may refer to a known festival dance or to dancing between two rows of onlookers.
literary: The chapter is built from dialogue. The friends speak (verse 1), the woman answers (verses 2-3), the man praises her (verses 4-10), someone, probably the woman, speaks of going down to the orchard (verses 11-12), and a group calls her back while another voice asks why they stare (verse 13). Identifying speakers is one of the chief difficulties of reading the Song, since Hebrew marks it mostly through grammatical gender. The man's praise in verses 5 to 7 repeats 4:1-3, and the question in verse 10, “Who is this…”, echoes 3:6 and anticipates 8:5. Verse 3 is a near reversal of 2:16: there “My beloved is mine”, and here she begins with her belonging to him. Verse 12 is one of the hardest lines in the Old Testament to translate, and older versions turned part of it into a personal name (Amminadib); modern versions differ widely.

outline.t: The friends ask where the beloved has gone
She knows: he is in his garden, and they belong to each other

doctrines.note: The Song celebrates the beauty of bodies, gardens, animals, and landscapes without apology. It assumes what Genesis 1 teaches: that God's physical world, including human attraction, is good. There is no suspicion here that the body is less spiritual than the soul.

Verse 3 states the mutual belonging at the heart of the book, and verses 8 and 9 set one unique beloved against a royal harem. Many readers see here the Bible's ideal of exclusive, faithful love, standing in quiet contrast to the many wives of Solomon's court.

words.note: Dod, beloved. The woman's usual word for the man, used five times in this chapter alone. It can also mean love or lovemaking in the plural (as in 1:2), and it sounds like the name David. The whole chapter turns on the question the friends ask about where the dod has gone.

Shulammite, the title given to the woman in verse 13, here only in the Bible. Its origin is uncertain: a woman from Shunem, a feminine partner name to Solomon (Shelomoh), or a name tied to shalom, peace. The last connects with 8:10, where she says she has become like one who brings peace.

Tam, complete or perfect, translated my perfect one in verse 9. The same word describes Job as blameless and Jacob as a quiet man. Here it means whole and flawless, the one who is everything to him, not a claim of moral sinlessness.

christ: The New Testament never quotes the Song of Songs, so any link to Christ is a matter of theme and of the church's long tradition of reading. Jewish interpreters from ancient times read the Song as a picture of the love between God and Israel, and Christian interpreters such as Origen in the third century and Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth read it as the love between Christ and the church or the soul. That reading has a biblical foundation even if individual details should not be pressed: the prophets call Israel God's bride, Paul says marriage is a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32), and Revelation ends with the marriage of the Lamb. The mutual belonging of verse 3 is a fitting echo of the covenant formula, I will be their God and they will be my people. A reader can honor the chapter first as a poem about human love and still see in faithful human love a small window onto the love of Christ, who seeks and does not let go.

hard.q: Is the Song of Songs about human love or about God's love, and how should it be read?
hard.a: There are several main readings, each with serious defenders. The allegorical reading, dominant in synagogue and church for many centuries, treats the book as a picture of God and Israel (in the Targum and rabbinic midrash) or Christ and the church or soul (in Origen, Bernard, and many others). Its strength is the Bible's frequent use of marriage for God's covenant; its weakness is that the details often became arbitrary, with every body part assigned a spiritual meaning. The natural or literal reading, now the most common among scholars, treats the Song as love poetry celebrating human desire and faithful love, whether as a collection of songs or as a loose drama with two main characters (Solomon and the woman) or three (the woman, her shepherd lover, and Solomon as a rival). Its strength is that it lets the text say what it plainly says. A typological reading tries to hold both together: the Song is first about human love, and because human marriage is itself meant to image God's covenant love, it can also point beyond itself. Whichever reading one takes, the book's presence in Scripture says that God cares about love between a man and a woman.

questions: The woman's confidence returns in verse 3 after a painful separation in chapter 5. What helps love survive seasons of distance or misunderstanding?
The man says his beloved is unique among sixty queens and eighty concubines. What does exclusive, faithful love offer that a crowd of options never can?
How does it change your view of God to find a book of love poetry in the Bible?
